content: 1. The European Community issued a directive on July 15, 1991, concerning the regulation and placement of plant protection products on the market. This directive has undergone subsequent amendments to ensure compliance with evolving standards. 2. On May 31, 1999, the European Parliament and Council adopted Directive 1999/45/EC, which aimed to harmonize the laws, regulations, and administrative provisions of Member States regarding the classification, packaging, and labeling of hazardous preparations. 3. Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, issued by the European Parliament and Council on December 16, 2008, established guidelines for the classification, labeling, and packaging of substances and mixtures. This regulation aligns with the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals. 4. Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, adopted on October 21, 2009, replaced earlier Council Directives 79/117/EEC and 91/414/EEC. It governs the placement of plant protection products on the market, ensuring safety and environmental protection. 5. The United States government, through the Code of Federal Regulations (Title 40, Part 156), established labeling requirements for pesticides and devices in 2010. These regulations are enforced by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). 6. In 2006, the Government of Canada published guidelines in the Canada Gazette (Vol. 140, Issue 13) to address pesticide labeling and safety measures. 7. CropLife International, in 2012, released a position paper on the implementation of the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) for the classification and labeling of crop protection products. This document emphasizes the importance of global standardization. 8. The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UN-ECE) published the 18th revised edition of the UN Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods – Model Regulations in 2013. These guidelines provide a framework for the safe transport of hazardous materials. 9. CropLife International also issued a technical monograph in 2008, detailing a catalog of pesticide formulation types and an international coding system. 10. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) developed ISO Standard 1750 in 1981, which provides common names for pesticides and agrochemicals, including subsequent amendments. 11. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) has published nomenclature guidelines for organic and inorganic chemistry, known as the Blue Book and Red Book, respectively. 12. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations released guidelines in 2012 for the prevention and management of pesticide resistance, emphasizing sustainable agricultural practices. 13. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued several key documents, including the 2009 classification of pesticides by hazard and guidelines for their application in public health. These include recommendations for vector control and procurement of public health pesticides. 14. Research studies, such as those by Wogalter et al. (1997) and Wang & Chi (2003), have explored the comprehension and retention of safety pictorials and the effects of hazardous material labeling on understanding. 15. The UK Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) published a report in 2002 on the impact of labeling schemes, highlighting their role in consumer safety and awareness. 16. The International Seed Federation (ISF) issued guidelines in 2014 for labeling treated seeds, ensuring proper handling and safety measures. 17. ISO Standard 11683 (1997) outlines requirements for tactile warnings of danger on packaging, while ISO/IEC Standard 18004 (2015) specifies QR code symbology for automatic identification and data capture. 18. Annexes in various guidelines provide detailed recommendations for print size, style, and precautionary statements on product labels. These include minimum font sizes, the use of bold and italic text for emphasis, and ensuring readability under practical conditions. 19. Signal words and hazard statements on pesticide labels are determined by the product's hazard classification, as outlined in the GHS Purple Book. Precautionary statements are often defined at the national level and aim to mitigate identified risks. 20. General precautionary statements for pesticide labels include instructions such as Read the label before use, Keep out of reach of children, and Wash after use. These statements are tailored to address specific hazards and risks associated with pesticides. 21. Additional precautionary measures address physical, health, and environmental hazards. For example, statements may include restrictions on worker entry into treated areas, protection of residents and consumers, and measures to prevent contamination of water sources and harm to non-target organisms. 22. Specific guidelines for storage and disposal of pesticides emphasize secure storage, proper labeling, and adherence to approved waste disposal practices. For instance, pesticides should always be stored in their original containers, and empty containers should not be reused. 23. Agricultural practices, such as the handling of treated seeds, require careful adherence to safety protocols. This includes avoiding contact with skin and respiratory tracts, using protective equipment, and ensuring proper incorporation of treated seeds into the soil.
